full.dental:
What's tested
  • The major glands and their hormones, and the three hormone classes with an example of each ("you'll need to know that there's 3 main types of hormones")
  • The oral findings of each disorder: acromegaly's growing jaw, hyper- and hypothyroidism, hyper- and hypoparathyroidism on the radiograph, Addison disease, Cushing syndrome, diabetes, and puberty, pregnancy and menopause
  • His clinical points: implants wait until growth stops, the recurrent laryngeal nerve in thyroid surgery, epinephrine in hyperthyroidism, extra steroid after a big procedure in Addison disease
  • The diabetic patient: his numbers (HbA1c above 7 is poorly controlled; a glucose under 60 needs sugar), the checks before treatment and the rescue for hypoglycemia: finger-stick, glucose rather than table sugar, glucagon if that fails
  • Recognizing three emergencies: thyroid storm (call 911), adrenal crisis and hypoglycemia
  • His three cases, which he walked through by asking the class: Graves disease, a type 2 diabetic who needs an extraction (and his pack-year question), and Addison disease with oral pigmentation

Dr. Chad Taylor (DMD, BSN) gave Lecture A on Friday, November 6, at 8 am. His deck, "Endocrine System Review", makes a fast pass through each gland, shows what its disorders look like in the mouth and how they change treatment, and ends with three patient cases. He added stories from his clinic and his years in surgery and quizzed the class through the cases. These notes follow his recording and his slides. Where he said something that another lecture in this exam teaches differently, the notes say which to use.

His learning objectives: describe the major endocrine glands and hormones; explain how hormones act and are regulated; recognize how endocrine disorders affect oral health and dental treatment; apply endocrine physiology to assessing and managing dental patients; and correlate endocrine dysfunction with common oral findings. Three of the five are about patients, so practice with the cases.

What the endocrine system does

The endocrine system regulates six jobs: growth and development, metabolism, reproduction, stress responses, calcium and phosphate homeostasis, and fluid and electrolyte balance. Every disorder later in the lecture is one of these jobs done too much or too little.

He contrasted it with the nervous system, which does similar work in a different way. Speed of response: the nervous system is always faster, because it works on electrical signals through nerves spread all over the body. The endocrine system releases its hormones into the bloodstream, and the blood takes time to carry them around. Duration of action: hormones act longer, and they also take longer to shut off, so when the endocrine system overreacts, the body takes longer to bring it back under control.

Hormone classes and how they act

"You'll need to know that there's 3 main types of hormones," he said: amines, such as epinephrine and norepinephrine; peptides, such as insulin; and steroids, such as estrogen or testosterone.

Hormones act through cell-surface receptors, often working through second messenger systems, or through intracellular receptors: steroids cross the cell membrane, act at the nucleus and turn on DNA transcription. Peptides such as insulin bind on the cell surface.

Most systems are held in range by negative feedback, much of it in the hypothalamus and pituitary: when a hormone builds up, the brain senses it and turns production down. His example: when testosterone spikes, the pituitary turns down the gonadotropin that drives it (he named FSH; Lectures 13 and 15 teach that LH drives the Leydig cells' testosterone, so use LH if a question asks). Aromatase balances it by converting testosterone to estrogen; a man taking large doses of testosterone, for bodybuilding say, can outrun it, and the imbalance raises his cardiovascular risk.

Keep feedback in mind for Addison disease, because it explains the oral pigmentation: when the adrenal cortex makes too little cortisol, nothing turns ACTH down, so ACTH rises.

The hypothalamus and pituitary

The hypothalamus and pituitary are the control center. The hypothalamus sends releasing and inhibiting hormones to the pituitary, and the anterior pituitary's hormones then drive the other glands: if you need more cortisol, the pituitary releases more ACTH.

HormoneMajor function
ACTHAdrenal cortex stimulation
TSHThyroid stimulation
GH (growth hormone)Growth regulation
FSH and LHReproductive function
ProlactinLactation

Growth hormone stays with you for life, but it is strongest in childhood and adolescence. What stops the long bones from growing is the sex hormones: at puberty the growth plates fuse, and growth hormone no longer lengthens them. He uses this in treatment planning. A 13- or 14-year-old boy who is growing hair on his upper lip is probably close to puberty and near his final height. If a patient lost a tooth at 10, he waits for growth to stop before placing an implant: an implant is fixed in the bone, and if the face is still growing, everything moves around it.

The posterior pituitary has two hormones. ADH conserves water. Too little ADH is diabetes insipidus: the kidneys let out far too much fluid, so the patient is very thirsty all the time. Don't confuse it with diabetes mellitus, the insulin disease: same first word, different hormone. Oxytocin, the "connection hormone" of delivery, is the other. His trivia: alcohol lowers ADH (so you urinate) and nicotine raises it.

Growth hormone excess: acromegaly

Too much growth hormone before puberty, while the long bones are still open, makes a person very tall, 7 feet or more. After puberty the long bones are fused, so they barely grow, and the condition is acromegaly. The hands and feet enlarge, but "look for the jaw in your patients": the mandible grows, so the bite changes, from a normal Class I to edge-to-edge or even a Class III malocclusion. The bigger arch leaves more room for the teeth, so diastemas open between them, and the tongue enlarges (macroglossia). Macroglossia also appears under hypothyroidism, so it is the jaw and the spacing that point to growth hormone.

The thyroid

The thyroid makes T3 and T4, regulated by TSH from the anterior pituitary. They act on metabolism, and the thyroid works like the body's thermostat, so thyroid disease shows in heat intolerance and in weight. That is why the two disorders are mirror images: too much hormone speeds the body up, and too little slows it down.

A surgical point he made from his years in the operating room: the recurrent laryngeal nerve runs through the thyroid area, and the first thing a surgeon does in a thyroidectomy or a parathyroidectomy is find it. Damage to it paralyzes half of the vocal cords, leaving a hoarse, raspy voice that is usually permanent.

Hyperthyroidism is something you will see only on occasion. He said it is generally associated with an adenoma, a tumor of the gland that makes too much hormone. (His own Graves case is the other cause, and Lecture 12a teaches that Graves disease is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism.) It brings weight loss, tachycardia and heat intolerance. For the dentist: the patient has increased sensitivity to epinephrine, so avoid excessive vasoconstrictor use in uncontrolled disease, since another stimulant raises an already fast heart rate and blood pressure; and in children, accelerated tooth eruption: if permanent teeth come in early, ask the family to have the child's thyroid checked.

Hypothyroidism you will see far more often. It brings fatigue, weight gain and at times bradycardia. It can delay eruption, but what you are more likely to see is macroglossia and delayed wound healing. Most of these patients take thyroid hormone to replace what they lack.

HyperthyroidismHypothyroidism
How often you'll see itOn occasionFar more often
WeightLossGain
Heart rateTachycardiaBradycardia
OtherHeat intoleranceFatigue
Eruption in childrenAcceleratedDelayed
Other dental pointsIncreased sensitivity to epinephrine; avoid excessive vasoconstrictor when uncontrolledMacroglossia; delayed wound healing

The epinephrine caution belongs to hyperthyroidism, not hypothyroidism. Statement questions like to move one finding to the other side, so learn this table as pairs: weight lost or gained, a fast or a slow heart, early or late eruption.

Thyroid storm

Thyroid storm, also called thyroid crisis or thyrotoxic crisis, is rare, but it happens: the gland releases a large amount of hormone in a short time. It is a life-threatening emergency. The signs are a high fever, a rapid heart rate, 140 or higher, agitation, anxiety, shakiness, nausea and even delirium. "If you start to see signs and symptoms of this, call 911." In his Graves case, the first thing he would check is the heart rate.

In the chair, thyroid storm can look like hypoglycemia, because both bring a racing pulse, shakiness and confusion. The fever and the high blood pressure point to thyroid storm. Sweating is on his hypoglycemia list, but a hyperthyroid patient sweats too, as the Exam 1 thyroid lecture taught, so it doesn't settle the question.

The parathyroids and calcium

There are four parathyroid glands, and their job is calcium homeostasis. In a parathyroidectomy, he said, surgeons usually leave the patient half of one gland, embedded in a neck muscle, so some tissue keeps managing calcium.

Three hormones keep blood calcium in range.

  • Parathyroid hormone, or PTH, is the fast-acting regulator, under negative feedback. It raises blood calcium three ways. At bone, he said, it inhibits osteoblasts and stimulates osteoclasts, so bone is resorbed. At the kidney, it increases calcium reabsorption. And it has the kidneys release calcitriol, active vitamin D, which makes the GI tract absorb more calcium. His summary: the body takes calcium from the bones, keeps what it already has, and absorbs more.
  • Vitamin D is the long-term regulator. We make it in the skin in an inactive form; the active form comes from the kidney, and it helps the gut absorb calcium.
  • Calcitonin works the other way. Increased blood calcium stimulates the thyroid to release calcitonin, which reverses PTH's effects on bone: "essentially the reverse of parathyroid hormone."

He said "inhibits osteoblasts, stimulates osteoclasts," as on his slide. If a question asks which cell PTH acts on, use Exam 1's mechanism: the PTH receptor is on the osteoblast, which then activates the osteoclasts through RANK ligand; calcitonin acts on the osteoclast itself. Both agree on the result: more osteoclast resorption, more calcium in the blood.

Hyperparathyroidism on the radiograph

Too much PTH means too much bone resorption, and at times osteoporosis. On radiographs, look for loss of the lamina dura. On a normal film, a thin white line outlines the socket: that is the lamina dura, the harder, denser bone the periodontal ligament attaches to. The thin dark line between it and the root is the PDL space. In hyperparathyroidism the white line is lost: the bone looks diffuse and gray right up to the tooth, with no definite outline.

You may also see brown tumors and tooth mobility. A brown tumor shows on a panoramic radiograph as a radiolucent area; his example sat in the bone below a premolar. If you find one, ask the patient about other symptoms and send them to their physician to be checked.

Hypoparathyroidism

Too little PTH means hypocalcemia, and because muscles need calcium to work, low calcium shows as neuromuscular irritability and tetany, muscles that lock up and don't relax. "You need to understand the calcium metabolism side of this, and also its effects on oral and maxillofacial bone."

The adrenal cortex

The cortex makes the two hormones he lists. Cortisol handles the stress response, immune regulation and glucose metabolism. Aldosterone handles sodium retention and potassium regulation. Patients on long-term corticosteroids show cortisol's effects, especially a higher blood glucose and a weaker immune system.

Addison disease is the deficiency. The adrenal cortex fails, and cortisol is the main hormone lacking, often with reduced aldosterone too. Clinically: hypotension, because the kidneys lose salt and the water goes with it, so blood volume falls; fatigue; and hyperpigmentation, brown and black patches on the gums and tongue. The more extensive form is diffuse oral melanosis. If you see these patches, have the patient checked.

Why the pigment? "I didn't really give you guys this," he said, so he told the class: with little cortisol, negative feedback no longer holds ACTH down, so ACTH production increases, and the extra ACTH stimulates melanocytes, darkening the skin and the oral mucosa. It is high ACTH, not cortisol, that colors the mouth.

Adrenal crisis is the emergency of Addison disease. It can be set off by stressful or lengthy surgical procedures, significant infection or trauma, and a missed steroid dose. Any stressful event, an extraction included, normally makes the body produce more corticosteroid, and these patients can't, so after a bigger procedure they may need supplemental corticosteroid, usually a larger dose than normal; agree on the dose with their physician first. The signs of a crisis are severe hypotension, weakness, confusion, loss of consciousness and shock.

Cushing syndrome is the other side: the body makes too much corticosteroid, and the patient looks like someone on long-term steroid therapy. Fat moves to the face and the back of the neck, giving a moon face and a buffalo hump, and there is hyperglycemia. In the mouth, plan for an increased infection risk and delayed healing.

Addison diseaseCushing syndrome
CortisolToo little (often with low aldosterone)Too much (or long-term steroid therapy)
Clinical featuresHypotension, fatigue, hyperpigmentationMoon face, buffalo hump, hyperglycemia
In the mouthBrown patches; diffuse oral melanosisIncreased infection risk, delayed healing
EmergencyAdrenal crisis; extra steroid after a big procedureNone listed

The adrenal medulla

The medulla makes epinephrine and norepinephrine, the fight-or-flight hormones: the heart speeds up, vessels constrict, the bronchioles dilate and the stomach stops moving. Its dental significance is vasoconstrictor use, the epinephrine in local anesthetics, and stress management during treatment.

His memory tool for cortex versus medulla: a corticosteroid is called that because it comes from the adrenal cortex. The medulla is epinephrine and norepinephrine.

The pancreas

The pancreas makes digestive enzymes too, but his focus is its two opposite hormones. Alpha cells make glucagon, which breaks down glycogen, the sugar stored in the liver and muscles, and drives gluconeogenesis: without food, the body makes its own glucose for the brain from muscle and triglycerides.

Metformin inhibits gluconeogenesis, and he drew a chair-side warning from it. A type 2 diabetic took her medicines but skipped breakfast to make the appointment. She has blocked her own glucose production and eaten nothing, so in his example she is at high risk of hypoglycemia in your chair; be ready with glucose if she turns sweaty or agitated. (Lecture 11 teaches that metformin alone rarely causes hypoglycemia; insulin and the secretagogues are the usual cause. Either way, ask about the meal.)

Beta cells make insulin, which moves glucose into muscle and fat cells. Excess glucose is stored first as glycogen, which has limited room, then as fat: insulin is the storage hormone.

Diabetes mellitus

Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune destruction of the beta cells. It usually starts young, and because the body makes no insulin, these patients need insulin injections to survive. Type 2 diabetes is insulin resistance: the cells' receptors don't respond to insulin, so the pancreas makes more, and these patients have hyperinsulinemia, higher than normal insulin, with a high blood glucose. In type 2 the insulin is ineffective, not deficient. His slides add that production may decline over time.

His numbers for the chair:

MeasureWhat it means
Finger-stick glucose under 60Hypoglycemia: give sugar
Fasting glucose well over 100May have diabetes: insulin isn't clearing the blood
HbA1c about 5 percentTypical for a person without diabetes
HbA1c below 7 (below 6 even better)Generally well controlled
HbA1c above 7Poorly controlled: much higher risk of implant failure and of periodontal disease; plan treatment accordingly

For diagnosis, use Lecture 11's cutoffs: prediabetes is an HbA1c of 5.7 to 6.4 percent or a fasting glucose of 100 to 125, and diabetes is 6.5 percent or 126 and above. He called an HbA1c above 5.3 a sign of risk for prediabetes. His 7 percent is the line for control in a patient who already has diabetes, and it is the number to know for this lecture.

The type 2 drugs he named: metformin; the sulfonylureas, which make the beta cells release more insulin; and newer drugs such as dapagliflozin (Farxiga), which acts on the sodium-glucose transporter in the kidney so the extra sugar is passed in the urine. Sugar in the urine feeds Candida and bacteria, so these patients have a higher risk of urinary tract infections.

The oral manifestations of diabetes are xerostomia (the most common, but not specific), candidiasis, burning mouth syndrome, delayed healing, and an increased risk of periodontal disease and of dental caries. Why the candidiasis and caries: saliva is filtered blood, so a high blood glucose puts more sugar in the saliva, which feeds Candida and Streptococcus mutans.

The periodontal connection is bidirectional. When diabetes worsens, periodontal disease worsens, and periodontal inflammation worsens glycemic control, so keeping their mouths clean, and their home care, matters to their diabetes.

Why does an uncontrolled diabetic heal poorly after an extraction? In class he named high glucose, poor immune function and decreased neutrophil function; his slides add poor blood supply and impaired collagen synthesis. His two dental concerns follow: delayed healing, so be prepared for a long recovery, and an increased risk of postoperative infection.

Managing the diabetic patient

WhenWhat he does
Before treatmentReview glycemic control: did they eat, did they take their medication, what is the HbA1c (above 7 means more risk)
SchedulingMorning appointments preferred; time procedures after meals and medications
During treatmentMonitor for hypoglycemia: sweating, tremors, confusion, tachycardia, agitation
Signs appearAsk permission, then check a finger-stick glucose with the office glucometer
Conscious patientA fast-acting carbohydrate: straight glucose works fastest
Oral glucose doesn't workIV dextrose if you have it; otherwise glucagon IM or subcutaneously
Unconscious patientActivate emergency protocols

Two warnings from a patient of his. Some patients wear a continuous glucose monitor, or CGM, a sensor taped to the arm. Some CGMs only read down to a certain level: his patient's stopped at 53, and her finger-stick was in the 30s. It took 10 or 12 packets of glucose gel to bring her back. She also took Mounjaro, and GLP-1 drugs slow the gut, so glucose given by mouth reaches the blood more slowly than you expect.

If oral glucose doesn't work and there is no IV, glucagon can be given intramuscularly or subcutaneously: it breaks down stored glycogen and drives gluconeogenesis, which may also override the metformin. It is a last-ditch option that often isn't on hand: the school's dental clinic doesn't stock it, and at about 480 dollars a dose it is the costliest item in an emergency kit.

Not all sugars are the same. Table sugar, sucrose, is half glucose and half fructose, and the body can't use fructose (or galactose) directly: the liver has to convert it to glucose first. Straight glucose needs less processing, so it raises the blood sugar faster.

Reproductive endocrinology

The sex hormones, estrogen, progesterone and testosterone, are driven by the pituitary, and their oral effects change with the stage of life. Pregnant women tend to have more gingival inflammation because their estrogen and progesterone are higher. Besides pregnancy gingivitis, he sees the pyogenic granuloma, or "pregnancy tumor", fairly often: an overgrowth of gum tissue, usually in the interproximal region. His explanation to patients: the body is on guard, and the gums overreact. At menopause the sex hormones fall, which brings xerostomia, altered taste and effects on bone, possibly osteoporosis.

Life stageOral effects
PubertyIncreased gingival inflammation
PregnancyPregnancy gingivitis; pyogenic granuloma, the "pregnancy tumor", usually interproximal
MenopauseXerostomia; altered taste; osteoporosis implications

Same finding, more than one cause

Several findings appear under more than one condition in this lecture. The rest of the history decides which one you are looking at.

FindingWhere it shows up
MacroglossiaGrowth hormone excess and hypothyroidism
Fast pulse, tremor, confusionHyperthyroidism and thyroid storm, and hypoglycemia
Delayed healingHypothyroidism, Cushing syndrome and diabetes
HyperglycemiaDiabetes, Cushing syndrome and long-term steroids
XerostomiaDiabetes and menopause
Increased caries riskDiabetes, and hyperthyroidism in his Graves case
HypotensionAddison disease and adrenal crisis

Three emergencies in the chair

Thyroid stormAdrenal crisisHypoglycemia
WhoUncontrolled hyperthyroidismAddison diseaseDiabetic patient, for example medication taken without the meal
Key signsHigh fever, heart rate 140 or higher, agitation, deliriumSevere hypotension, weakness, confusion, shockSweating, tremors, confusion, tachycardia; glucose under 60
Blood pressureHighSeverely lowNot on his list
What he says to doCall 911Know the triggers (long or stressful surgery, infection or trauma, missed steroids); extra steroid after a big procedure, dose set with the physicianFinger-stick; glucose by mouth if awake; IV dextrose or glucagon if that fails; emergency protocols if unconscious

His case: Lucilla, a racing heart

A 42-year-old woman comes in for a routine cleaning and says her heart feels like it's racing. She was recently diagnosed with Graves disease and takes methimazole. She has lost weight despite a bigger appetite ("a warning bell automatically"), can't tolerate heat, has a tremor and anxiety, and her thyroid gland is enlarged. Her blood pressure is 142 over 88 and her pulse is 112.

His answers: the gland is the thyroid, and the elevated hormones are T3 and T4. Use epinephrine cautiously: she is already overstimulated, and another stimulant could put her at risk. In the mouth: accelerated eruption in younger patients, more caries, burning mouth, and the tremor ("try doing dentistry on a moving object"). The emergency to fear is thyroid storm; the first thing he would check is her heart rate, usually over 140 in a storm.

His case: Proximo, an extraction in an uncontrolled diabetic

A 68-year-old man needs non-restorable mandibular first molars extracted. He has had type 2 diabetes for 22 years, has hypertension, takes his metformin irregularly, reports frequent thirst and urination, and smokes a pack a day. His blood pressure is 148 over 92, pulse 84. In the mouth: generalized moderate periodontal disease, delayed healing of a previous extraction site, dry mouth and multiple carious lesions. His fasting blood glucose is 220 milligrams per deciliter, and his HbA1c is 9.8 percent.

His quick quiz on the smoking: the pack-year history is packs per day times years smoked, so one pack a day for 40 years is 40 pack-years. "Don't forget that. You'll need to know that next year for clinic."

His answers: the organ is the pancreas, and the hormone is insulin, most likely ineffective rather than deficient, because type 2 patients are typically hyperinsulinemic. His periodontal disease is worse because of impaired healing and more food for the bacteria. Before the extraction, be prepared for delayed wound healing, verify his glycemic control and time the procedure after his meal and medication.

His case: Commodus, brown patches in the mouth

A 25-year-old man asks about pigmentation in his mouth. He was diagnosed with Addison disease three years ago and has chronic fatigue, weight loss, dizziness when he stands up, and muscle weakness. The exam shows diffuse brown pigmentation of the buccal mucosa and gingiva, and his blood pressure is 90 over 60.

His answers: the affected gland is the adrenal cortex, not the medulla, which makes epinephrine and norepinephrine. The deficient hormone is cortisol, often with reduced aldosterone, but cortisol is the main worry. The pigment comes from increased ACTH stimulating melanocytes. Surgery, infection or a missed dose could set off an adrenal crisis, and he may need extra corticosteroid after a bigger procedure. In a crisis, expect severe hypotension (his pressure is already low), weakness, confusion and shock.

His deck ends with a "Words of Warning" slide, an image he showed with only "Gentlemen, remember that." Nothing in it is tested.

plain.dental:
What's tested
  • Which gland makes which hormone, and the three kinds of hormones
  • What each hormone problem looks like in the mouth and on the X-ray
  • What to do for these patients in the chair, especially diabetics: his numbers and how to fix low sugar
  • How to spot thyroid storm, adrenal crisis and low blood sugar
  • His three patient cases

Dr. Taylor's lecture is a review of the endocrine system for dentists. For each gland: what it makes, what goes wrong, and what you see in the mouth. Then three patients. These notes follow his recording and slides.

The basics

Hormones control growth, metabolism, reproduction, stress, calcium, and fluid balance. They travel in the blood, so they are slower than nerves, but they last longer and take longer to shut off.

Three kinds, and he said you need to know them: amine (epinephrine, norepinephrine), peptide (insulin), steroid (estrogen, testosterone). Peptides like insulin bind on the cell surface. Steroids go inside the cell, to the nucleus.

Negative feedback keeps hormones in range. When a gland's hormone gets low, the signal from the pituitary goes up.

Pituitary

The hypothalamus is the boss of the pituitary. The front of the pituitary makes ACTH for the adrenal cortex, TSH for the thyroid, GH for growth, FSH and LH for reproduction, and prolactin for milk. The back makes ADH, which saves water, and oxytocin. Too little ADH is diabetes insipidus: the kidneys dump water and the patient is always thirsty. That is not the sugar diabetes.

Growth hormone stays all your life. Sex hormones at puberty close the growth plates, so the long bones stop growing. Wait until a young patient has stopped growing before placing an implant, or the face grows around it.

Too much growth hormone before puberty makes a very tall person. After puberty it is acromegaly. Watch the jaw: it grows, the bite slides toward Class III, gaps open between the teeth, and the tongue gets big.

Thyroid

The thyroid makes T3 and T4, under TSH from the pituitary. They run metabolism and body heat. In thyroid surgery, the surgeon first finds the recurrent laryngeal nerve: damage it and the patient is left hoarse, usually for good.

Too much (hyperthyroid): weight loss, fast heart, always hot. Teeth come in early in kids. These patients are extra sensitive to epinephrine, so go easy on the vasoconstrictor if the disease isn't controlled.

Too little (hypothyroid), which you'll see far more often: tired, weight gain, slow heart. Teeth can come in late; more often you see a big tongue and slow healing.

Memory trick: hyper is fast, hypo is slow. Fast heart and early teeth, or slow heart and late teeth.

Thyroid storm is rare: the gland dumps a lot of hormone at once. High fever, a heart rate of 140 or more, agitated, shaky, nauseated, delirious, high blood pressure. It is life-threatening: call 911.

Calcium

PTH from the four parathyroids raises calcium fast. It makes bone break down (osteoclasts), makes the kidneys hold on to calcium, and has the kidneys make active vitamin D so the gut absorbs calcium.

Vitamin D is the slow, long-term controller. It is activated in the kidney.

Calcitonin comes from the thyroid when calcium is high. It undoes PTH.

Too much PTH: bone breaks down. On the X-ray you lose the lamina dura, the thin white line of bone around each root. You can get brown tumors, which look dark (radiolucent), and the teeth get loose. Send the patient to their doctor.

Too little PTH: calcium drops. Muscles twitch and lock up (tetany).

Adrenal glands

The outer part, the cortex, makes cortisol (stress, immune system, sugar) and aldosterone (keeps sodium, handles potassium). The inner part, the medulla, makes epinephrine and norepinephrine. That matters for the vasoconstrictor in your anesthetic and for keeping patients calm. Trick: a corticosteroid comes from the cortex.

Addison disease: not enough cortisol. Low blood pressure, tired, dark skin, and brown patches in the mouth. Why brown? Low cortisol lets ACTH climb, and ACTH turns on the pigment cells.

Adrenal crisis is Addison's emergency. It can be set off by a long or stressful surgery, a bad infection or injury, or a missed steroid dose. After a big procedure the patient may need extra steroid; ask their doctor how much. Look for very low blood pressure, weakness, confusion, passing out and shock.

Cushing syndrome: too much cortisol, and it looks just like long-term steroid pills. Round "moon" face, a hump between the shoulders, high blood sugar. In the mouth: more infections and slow healing.

Pancreas and diabetes

Alpha cells make glucagon, which breaks down stored sugar and makes new sugar. Beta cells make insulin, which moves sugar into cells and stores it.

Type 1: the immune system destroys the beta cells, so the patient needs insulin shots. Type 2: the body resists insulin, and insulin levels run high. The insulin is there but doesn't work.

His numbers: a finger-stick under 60 means give sugar. An HbA1c above 7 means poor control, with more implant failures and more gum disease. Below 7 is good control; most people without diabetes run about 5.

Metformin stops the liver from making sugar. A diabetic who took it and skipped breakfast can go low in your chair.

In the mouth, diabetes brings dry mouth, thrush (candidiasis), burning mouth, slow healing, more gum disease and more cavities. Saliva comes from the blood, so high blood sugar means sugary saliva that feeds yeast and cavity germs.

Gum disease and diabetes make each other worse. Keep the mouth clean.

Why extractions heal slowly: high sugar, weak immune cells (neutrophils), poor blood supply and poor collagen. So expect slow healing and infection.

The diabetic patient in your chair

Before: check how well the sugar is controlled (HbA1c). Ask if they ate and took their medicine. Book mornings.

During: watch for low sugar: sweating, shaking, confusion, a fast heart. Check a finger-stick (ask first). A glucose monitor on the arm may not read very low numbers, so check anyway.

If they're awake, give straight glucose. Table sugar is half fructose, which the liver has to convert first, so glucose works faster. Drugs like Mounjaro slow the stomach, so sugar by mouth works slowly. If it fails: IV sugar, or a glucagon shot. If they pass out, activate emergency protocols.

Low sugar or thyroid storm? Both shake and race. Fever and high blood pressure mean thyroid storm.

Sex hormones

Puberty: gums get more inflamed. Pregnancy: more estrogen and progesterone, so pregnancy gingivitis and the pyogenic granuloma, the "pregnancy tumor," a lump of gum tissue usually between two teeth. Menopause: dry mouth, changed taste, and weaker bones.

His three patients

Lucilla, Graves disease, heart racing, pulse 112: the thyroid is overactive, T3 and T4 are high. Go easy on epinephrine. Look for early eruption in the young, cavities, burning mouth, and a tremor that gets in the way. The danger is thyroid storm: check her heart rate first.

Proximo, type 2 diabetic for 22 years, skips his metformin, glucose 220, HbA1c 9.8 percent, needs extractions, smokes a pack a day: the problem is insulin that doesn't work. Expect slow healing, check his control first, and time the visit after his meal and medicine. Pack-years are packs a day times years: a pack a day for 40 years is 40 pack-years.

Commodus, Addison disease, brown patches in the mouth, blood pressure 90 over 60: the adrenal cortex is failing and cortisol is low. High ACTH causes the brown color. Long surgery, infection or a missed steroid dose can set off an adrenal crisis, and he may need extra steroid after a big procedure.

Some CGMs only read down to a certain level: his patient's stopped at 53, and her finger-stick was in the 30s. It took 10 or 12 packets of glucose gel to bring her back. She also took Mounjaro, and GLP-1 drugs slow the gut, so glucose given by mouth reaches the blood more slowly than you expect.

Not all sugars are the same. Table sugar, sucrose, is half glucose and half fructose, and the body can't use fructose (or galactose) directly: the liver has to convert it to glucose first. Straight glucose needs less processing, so it raises the blood sugar faster.

Metformin inhibits gluconeogenesis, and he drew a chair-side warning from it. A type 2 diabetic took her medicines but skipped breakfast to make the appointment. She has blocked her own glucose production and eaten nothing, so in his example she is at high risk of hypoglycemia in your chair; be ready with glucose if she turns sweaty or agitated. 3 Hyperthyroidism and Graves disease (his first case): epinephrine caution, and thyroid storm (fever, pulse 140 or more; call 911)

Know this
  • Thyroid storm: high fever, a pulse of 140 or more, agitation and delirium in uncontrolled hyperthyroidism; call 911.

Thyroid storm, also called thyroid crisis or thyrotoxic crisis, is rare, but it happens: the gland releases a large amount of hormone in a short time. It is a life-threatening emergency. The signs are a high fever, a rapid heart rate, 140 or higher, agitation, anxiety, shakiness, nausea and even delirium. "If you start to see signs and symptoms of this, call 911." In his Graves case, the first thing he would check is the heart rate.

4 Addison disease (his third case): oral pigment from high ACTH, adrenal crisis triggers and signs, extra corticosteroid after a big procedure; Cushing syndrome and long-term steroids

Flagged in the recording · 5 questions in the bank

Know this
  • An Addison patient can't raise cortisol for surgical stress: know the crisis triggers (long surgery, infection or trauma, a missed dose) and plan extra steroid with the physician.

Adrenal crisis is the emergency of Addison disease. It can be set off by stressful or lengthy surgical procedures, significant infection or trauma, and a missed steroid dose. Any stressful event, an extraction included, normally makes the body produce more corticosteroid, and these patients can't, so after a bigger procedure they may need supplemental corticosteroid, usually a larger dose than normal; agree on the dose with their physician first. The signs of a crisis are severe hypotension, weakness, confusion, loss of consciousness and shock.

6 Acromegaly's growing jaw (Class I to Class III, diastemas, macroglossia); growth plates fused by the sex hormones, and implant timing

Flagged in the recording · 4 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Acromegaly in an adult shows the dentist a growing mandible: a bite moving from Class I to edge-to-edge or Class III, new diastemas and a large tongue.
  • The sex hormones of puberty fuse the growth plates; plan a young patient's implant for after growth stops.

Growth hormone stays with you for life, but it is strongest in childhood and adolescence. What stops the long bones from growing is the sex hormones: at puberty the growth plates fuse, and growth hormone no longer lengthens them. He uses this in treatment planning. A 13- or 14-year-old boy who is growing hair on his upper lip is probably close to puberty and near his final height. If a patient lost a tooth at 10, he waits for growth to stop before placing an implant: an implant is fixed in the bone, and if the face is still growing, everything moves around it.

Too much growth hormone before puberty, while the long bones are still open, makes a person very tall, 7 feet or more. After puberty the long bones are fused, so they barely grow, and the condition is acromegaly. The hands and feet enlarge, but "look for the jaw in your patients": the mandible grows, so the bite changes, from a normal Class I to edge-to-edge or even a Class III malocclusion. The bigger arch leaves more room for the teeth, so diastemas open between them, and the tongue enlarges (macroglossia). Macroglossia also appears under hypothyroidism, so it is the jaw and the spacing that point to growth hormone.

7 The three hormone classes with examples, receptors, and endocrine versus nervous signaling

Flagged in the recording · 3 questions in the bank

He contrasted it with the nervous system, which does similar work in a different way. Speed of response: the nervous system is always faster, because it works on electrical signals through nerves spread all over the body. The endocrine system releases its hormones into the bloodstream, and the blood takes time to carry them around. Duration of action: hormones act longer, and they also take longer to shut off, so when the endocrine system overreacts, the body takes longer to bring it back under control.

8 Diabetes: type 1 versus type 2 (insulin ineffective, not deficient), oral manifestations and the sugar in saliva, the two-way periodontal link, SGLT2 drugs and UTIs

The oral manifestations of diabetes are xerostomia (the most common, but not specific), candidiasis, burning mouth syndrome, delayed healing, and an increased risk of periodontal disease and of dental caries. Why the candidiasis and caries: saliva is filtered blood, so a high blood glucose puts more sugar in the saliva, which feeds Candida and Streptococcus mutans.

  • Thyroid and parathyroid surgery puts the recurrent laryngeal nerve at risk: damage leaves a hoarse, raspy voice, usually for good.

A surgical point he made from his years in the operating room: the recurrent laryngeal nerve runs through the thyroid area, and the first thing a surgeon does in a thyroidectomy or a parathyroidectomy is find it. Damage to it paralyzes half of the vocal cords, leaving a hoarse, raspy voice that is usually permanent.

11 Pituitary hormones (ADH and diabetes insipidus), alpha and beta cells, and the adrenal medulla

Objectives · 3 questions in the bank

The posterior pituitary has two hormones. ADH conserves water. Too little ADH is diabetes insipidus: the kidneys let out far too much fluid, so the patient is very thirsty all the time. Don't confuse it with diabetes mellitus, the insulin disease: same first word, different hormone. Oxytocin, the "connection hormone" of delivery, is the other. His trivia: alcohol lowers ADH (so you urinate) and nicotine raises it.
